title: Modelling Evidence-Based Practice in Initial Teacher Training https://repec-cepeo.ucl.ac.uk/cepeow/cepeowp23-09.pdf https://tipsforteachers.co.uk/research-modelling-evidence-based-practice-in-initial-teacher-training/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), February 21, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers Ambition Institute research led by Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, and Stefanie Meliss testing whether video modeling improves trainee teachers' skills, knowledge, and self-efficacy in a specific technique — questioning for retrieval. Using classroom simulations, the study compares restudying theory, watching a video model, and watching a model that explicitly integrates the underlying theory. Results showed models improved skills relative to no model at all, giving causal evidence that watching demonstrations of good practice measurably helps trainees. Barton draws out practical implications for teacher educators: build video libraries of evidence-based technique, retrospectively narrate the rationale behind what's modeled so trainees don't miss the valuable parts, and support trainees in reintegrating an isolated modeled technique back into the flow of a real lesson.
points: Video models of good teaching practice measurably improved trainee teachers' skills relative to no model at all — modeling isn't just intuitively helpful, it has causal evidence behind it.
Teacher educators should consider building video libraries of evidence-based technique demonstrations that trainees can access repeatedly, not just watch once.

When a model shows a full authentic lesson sequence rather than an isolated technique, educators need to retrospectively highlight and explain the rationale for specific moves — otherwise trainees can miss what made the modeled practice valuable.
Trainees need explicit support reintegrating a technique they've seen modeled in isolation back into the messier flow of a real classroom's pedagogical and curricular sequence.
quotes: Results showed that models improved skills relative to no model
Consider incorporating models into professional development to improve teaching skills. This may help teachers bridge the gap between theory and practice in the classroom.

Professional development programs might incorporate video libraries demonstrating good practice, or develop publicly available video libraries of evidence-based teaching techniques available to all trainees.
When modeling larger lesson sequences in authentic settings, teacher educators may need to retrospectively highlight certain aspects of their practice and explain the rationale to the trainee.
Teachers may need support to reintegrate the specific techniques depicted in models into the flow of real-world pedagogical and curricular sequences.
